newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU Court annuls Commission pension funds paper.
newsitem.headline: EU Court annuls Commission pension funds paper.

text.p: The European Court of Justice annuled on Thursday a 1994 European Commission policy document on the investment of pension funds saying it smacked of an attempt to create binding rules through the back door.

The court found that the Commission acted outside the scope of its authority when it adopted and published a communication aimed at creating a single market for the $1.3 trillion European pension fund industry.

The communication was issued shortly after the Commission was forced to withdraw a draft directive on the freedom of management and investment of pension funds in the face of strong opposition from all but three EU countries -- Britain, Ireland and the Netherlands.
France brought the issue to the court, supported by Spain, and successfully argued the Commission's published communication created new legal effects for member states.
The court said the Commission was "not empowered to adopt an act" which "intended to have legal effects of its own, distinct from those already provided for by the treaty."

The ruling is an apparent setback for the European pension funds industry which has to contend with a vast array of investment restrictions, like minimum investment requirements in local shares and government debt.

But industry representatives have played down the widely expected decision saying that national capitals' and particularly France's approach to privately run pension schemes has considerably evolved in the last few years due to the limits of the state pension regimes.
"The pressure for changes is so enormous...I think the attitude of France is no longer the same," Koen de Ryck, secretary-general of the European Federation for Retirement Provision, said recently.

The Commission was unhappy with the decision, but noted the court did not rule against a single market in the pension fund area, only against the procedure it used, the spokeswoman for Internal Market and Financial Services Commissioner Mario Monti said.

Monti is planning to relaunch the debate, taking advantage of EU countries' desperate efforts to reduce their public deficits, including the huge gap in their social security budgets, to meet the tough requirements for the European single currency.
A green paper on pension funds is expected in May, Monti's spokeswoman told a news conference.
